claim: HHV-6A and HHV-6B are ubiquitous betaherpesviruses, infecting the majority of the human population.
source: Human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) A and B are ubiquitous betaherpesviruses, infecting the majority of the human population.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction regarding HHV-6B infecting more than 90% of the human population (Zerr et al., 2005).

claim: HHV-6A and HHV-6B encompass large genomes.
source: They encompass large genomes and our understanding of their protein coding potential is far from complete.
evidence: The manuscript states the genomes are 160 kb in length (Lindquester and Pellett, 1991; Martin et al., 1991).

claim: The study identified hundreds of new open reading frames (ORFs) in HHV-6A and HHV-6B, including upstream ORFs (uORFs) and internal ORFs (iORFs).
source: Here, we employ ribosome-profiling and systematic transcript-analysis to experimentally define HHV-6 translation products. We identify hundreds of new open reading frames (ORFs), including upstream ORFs (uORFs) and internal ORFs (iORFs), generating a complete unbiased atlas of HHV-6 proteome.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and it is supported by data presented in Figure 6B showing 268 novel ORFs in HHV-6A and 216 in HHV-6B.

claim: uORFs are enriched in late viral genes of betaherpesviruses.
source: We show uORFs are enriched in late viral genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7D showing enrichment of uORFs in late genes for HHV-6A, HHV-6B, and HCMV (p-value < 0.01).

claim: The study identified three highly abundant HHV-6 encoded long non-coding RNAs.
source: We identified three highly abundant HHV-6 encoded long non-coding RNAs, one of which generates a non-polyadenylated stable intron appearing to be a conserved feature of betaherpesviruses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 5 showing the three lncRNAs and their expression levels.

claim: One HHV-6 lncRNA generates a non-polyadenylated stable intron that is a conserved feature of betaherpesviruses.
source: We identified three highly abundant HHV-6 encoded long non-coding RNAs, one of which generates a non-polyadenylated stable intron appearing to be a conserved feature of betaherpesviruses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 showing the stable intron of lncRNA3 and its conservation in HCMV and MCMV (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: HHV-6A was suspected to associate with neurodegenerative disease such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: While HHV-6A remains poorly epidemiologically characterized, it was suspected to associate with neurodegenerative disease such as Alzheimer's disease (Allnutt et al., under review; Braun et al., 1997; Eimer et al., 2018; Leibovitch and Jacobson, 2014; Prusty et al., 2018b; Readhead et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: HHV-6B infects more than 90% of the human population.
source: HHV-6B is known to infect more than 90% of the human population (Zerr et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zerr et al., 2005.

claim: HHV-6B is the causative agent of Roseola Infantum.
source: HHV-6B is known to infect more than 90% of the human population (Zerr et al., 2005) and was found to be the causative agent of Roseola Infantum, leading to febrile seizures in more than 10% of acute infections (De Bolle et al., 2005; Hall et al., 1994; Yamanishi et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: HHV-6B causes febrile seizures in more than 10% of acute infections.
source: HHV-6B is known to infect more than 90% of the human population (Zerr et al., 2005) and was found to be the causative agent of Roseola Infantum, leading to febrile seizures in more than 10% of acute infections (De Bolle et al., 2005; Hall et al., 1994; Yamanishi et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: HHV-6A and HHV-6B establish lifelong latent infection in their hosts.
source: Both HHV-6A and HHV-6B, like all herpesviruses, establish a lifelong latent infection in their hosts (Kondo et al., 1991; Luppi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is consistent with established knowledge about herpesviruses.

claim: HHV-6 latency is established in multiple cell types, where the viral genome is integrated into host chromosomes between telomeres and subtelomeres.
source: HHV-6 latency is established in multiple cell types, where the viral genome is integrated into host chromosomes between telomeres and subtelomeres (Arbuckle et al., 2013; Braun et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: In approximately 1% of the population worldwide HHV-6 is integrated in every cell in the body and inherited due to integration of the viral genome in germline cells.
source: Remarkably, in approximately 1% of the population worldwide HHV-6 is integrated in every cell in the body, and inherited, due to integration of the viral genome in germline cells (Clark, 2016; Pellett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: HHV-6 reactivation is a common cause of encephalitis.
source: HHV-6 reactivation is a common cause of encephalitis, and has been associated with several diseases including multiple sclerosis, hepatitis, pneumonitis and graft-versus-host disease (Braun et al., 1997; Caselli and Di Luca, 2007; De Bolle et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: HHV-6 reactivation has been associated with multiple sclerosis, hepatitis, pneumonitis and graft-versus-host disease.
source: HHV-6 reactivation is a common cause of encephalitis, and has been associated with several diseases including multiple sclerosis, hepatitis, pneumonitis and graft-versus-host disease (Braun et al., 1997; Caselli and Di Luca, 2007; De Bolle et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The genomes of HHV-6A and HHV-6B consist of large linear double stranded DNA molecules, 160 kb in length, containing a unique segment flanked by direct repeats.
source: The genomes of HHV-6A and HHV-6B, similar to those of other herpesviruses, consist of large linear double stranded DNA molecules, 160 kb in length, containing a unique segment flanked by direct repeats (Lindquester and Pellett, 1991; Martin et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Traditional annotation of HHV-6 coding capacity has relied on ORF-based analyses using canonical translational start and stop sequences and arbitrary size restriction, resulting in a list of around 100 ORFs for each virus.
source: The annotation of HHV-6 coding capacity has traditionally relied on open reading frame (ORF)-based analyses using canonical translational start and stop sequences and arbitrary size restriction to demarcate putative protein coding genes, resulting in a list of around 100 ORFs for each virus (Dominguez et al., 1999; Gompels et al., 1995; Gravel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published annotations.

claim: Genome-wide analysis of herpesviruses using RNA sequencing revealed very complex transcriptomes.
source: In recent years, genome wide-analysis of herpesviruses using short RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) reads, and recently also direct and long-read RNA-seq revealed very complex transcriptomes (Balázs et al., 2018; Balázs et al., 2017; Depledge et al., 2019; Gatherer et al., 2011; Kara et al., 2019; O'Grady et al., 2019; O'Grady et al., 2016; Tombácz et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Genome-wide mapping of translation in herpesviruses revealed hundreds of new viral ORFs.
source: In recent years, genome wide-analysis of herpesviruses using short RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) reads, and recently also direct and long-read RNA-seq revealed very complex transcriptomes (Balázs et al., 2018; Balázs et al., 2017; Depledge et al., 2019; Gatherer et al., 2011; Kara et al., 2019; O'Grady et al., 2019; O'Grady et al., 2016; Tombácz et al., 2017), and combined with genome-wide mapping of translation, revealed hundreds of new viral ORFs (Arias et al., 2014; Bencun et al., 2018; Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012; Whisnant et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The study applied ribosome profiling and RNA-seq to HSB-2 and Molt-3 cells infected for 72 hr with HHV-6A strain GS and HHV-6B strain Z29, respectively.
source: Here, we employ ribosome-profiling and systematic transcript-analysis to experimentally define HHV-6 translation products.
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The study prepared three different ribosome-profiling libraries for each virus using lactimidomycin (LTM), harringtonine (Harr), and cycloheximide (CHX).
source: For each virus we mapped genome-wide translation events by preparing three different ribosome-profiling libraries (Ribo-seq). Two Ribo-seq libraries facilitate mapping of translation initiation sites, by treating cells with lactimidomycin (LTM) or harringtonine (Harr), drugs that inhibit translation initiation in distinct mechanisms and lead to accumulation of ribosomes at translation initiation sites (Figure 1A and Ingolia et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012). The third Ribo-seq library was prepared from cells treated with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX), and gives a snap-shot of actively translating ribosomes across the body of the translated ORF (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LTM and Harr treatments lead to accumulation of ribosomes at translation initiation sites.
source: Two Ribo-seq libraries facilitate mapping of translation initiation sites, by treating cells with lactimidomycin (LTM) or harringtonine (Harr), drugs that inhibit translation initiation in distinct mechanisms and lead to accumulation of ribosomes at translation initiation sites (Figure 1A and Ingolia et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in the data (Figure 1A).

claim: CHX treatment gives a snap-shot of actively translating ribosomes across the body of the translated ORF.
source: The third Ribo-seq library was prepared from cells treated with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX), and gives a snap-shot of actively translating ribosomes across the body of the translated ORF (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with established knowledge about CHX.

claim: The RNA-seq protocol used allows identification of transcription start sites (TSSs) due to a strong overrepresentation of fragments that start at the 5' end of transcripts.
source: In parallel, we used a tailored RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) protocol which on top of quantification of RNA levels allows identification of transcription start sites (TSSs) due to a strong overrepresentation of fragments that start at the 5' end of transcripts, as well as detection of polyadenylation sites (Figure 1A and Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and demonstrated in the data.

claim: The RNA-seq protocol used allows detection of polyadenylation sites.
source: In parallel, we used a tailored RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) protocol which on top of quantification of RNA levels allows identification of transcription start sites (TSSs) due to a strong overrepresentation of fragments that start at the 5' end of transcripts, as well as detection of polyadenylation sites (Figure 1A and Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and demonstrated in the data.

claim: The study found many misannotations of previously annotated ORFs (10 in HHV-6A and 11 in HHV-6B).
source: Comparing to previously annotated ORFs, we found many misannotations (10 and 11, in HHV-6A and HHV-6B respectively)
evidence: This is based on comparison of Ribo-seq data to previous annotations.

claim: The study found novel un-annotated ORFs (278 in HHV-6A and 227 in HHV-6B).
source: Comparing to previously annotated ORFs, we found many misannotations (10 and 11, in HHV-6A and HHV-6B respectively) and novel un-annotated ORFs (278 and 227, in HHV-6A and HHV-6B respectively).
evidence: This is based on Ribo-seq data analysis and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Many of the new ORFs are conserved between HHV-6A and HHV-6B.
source: Importantly, many of these new ORFs are conserved between HHV-6A and HHV-6B, validating our approach, and emphasizing the high similarity between these two viruses.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8A showing correlation between the number of iORFs and uORFs in homolog ORFs.

claim: Translation of the U30 gene initiates at an AUG 411 bp downstream of the previously annotated start in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B, resulting in a 946 amino acid long protein.
source: One example of misannotation is the U30 gene, an essential viral gene coding for an inner tegument protein (Nicholas and Martin, 1994). We found translation of this gene to initiate at an AUG 411 bp downstream of the previously annotated start, in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B, resulting in a 946 amino acid (aa) long protein (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The new U30 annotations include the C-terminal domain which was shown to interact with the large tegument protein in the HSV-1 homolog.
source: Importantly, the new annotations include the C-terminal domain which was shown to interact with the large tegument protein in the HSV-1 homolog (Richards et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: A 32 amino acid upstream overlapping ORF (uoORF) is coded by the U48 transcript, initiates upstream of the U48 canonical ORF and partially overlaps it.
source: For example, a short 32 aa ORF was found to initiate upstream of the envelope protein gene U48 (Figure 2B). This ORF partially overlaps the U48 gene, making it an upstream overlapping ORF (uoORF).
evidence: This is based on Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: uoORFs are known to have repressive regulatory effects conserved across vertebrates.
source: Since uoORFs are known to have repressive regulatory effects conserved across vertebrates (Johnstone et al., 2016), this novel ORF likely negatively regulates the translation of U48.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The U48 uoORF likely negatively regulates the translation of U48.
source: Since uoORFs are known to have repressive regulatory effects conserved across vertebrates (Johnstone et al., 2016), this novel ORF likely negatively regulates the translation of U48.
evidence: This is inferred from established knowledge about uoORFs and the observation of the uoORF in U48.

claim: Translation of two very short (<20 aa) uORFs from the 5'UTR of U36 was found.
source: The packaging gene U36 is an example of a gene for which we found translation of two very short (<20 aa) uORFs from its 5'UTR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: An internal ORF (iORF) initiating out-of-frame inside the coding region of U36 was identified.
source: In addition, we identified translation of an internal ORF (iORF), initiating out-of-frame, inside the coding region of U36 (Figure 2C), leading to translation of a novel ORF.
evidence: This is based on Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Two iORFs were observed in the U84 gene, one out-of-frame and another in-frame starting at an AUG downstream of the U84 start-codon.
source: In the U84 gene we observed two iORFs, one of them out-of-frame possibly regulating the downstream ORF, and another in-frame, starting at an AUG downstream of the U84 start-codon and ending in the same stop-codon, resulting in a truncated version of U84 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The study detected 24 out of 26 annotated HHV-6A splice junctions and all 24 annotated HHV-6B splice junctions.
source: We were able to detect 24 out of 26 annotated HHV-6A splice junctions and all 24 annotated HHV-6B splice junctions.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The study identified 37 novel splice junctions in HHV-6A and 44 in HHV-6B.
source: Furthermore, we identified 37 novel splice junctions in HHV-6A and 44 in HHV-6B (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Some of the novel splice junctions identified in HHV-6A were recently reported in HHV-6B and are confirmed here for both viruses (U19, U83, and all splice forms of U79).
source: Some of the novel splice junctions identified in HHV-6A were recently reported in HHV-6B and are confirmed here for both viruses (U19, U83, and all splice forms of U79, Greninger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a recent publication.

claim: Many of the novel splice junctions seem to belong to one long transcript composed of several short exons separated by long introns, spanning the U42-U57 locus.
source: Interestingly, many of the novel splice junctions seem to belong to one long transcript composed of several short exons separated by long introns, spanning the U42-U57 locus (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A splice junction between the HHV-6B U7 and U8 indicates that they are fused to one translation product, similar to the HHV-6A U7.
source: For example, a splice junction between the HHV-6B U7 and U8 indicates that they are fused to one translation product, similar to the HHV-6A U7 (Dominguez et al., 1999; Gompels et al., 1995; Gravel et al., 2013 and Figure 3—supplement figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—supplement figure 1A and supported by citations.

claim: A splice junction in the HHV-6A U13 gene indicates that the U12 and U13 proteins share their N-terminal domain.
source: Another splice junction in the HHV-6A U13 gene indicates that the U12 and U13 proteins share their N-terminal domain (Figure 3—supplement figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—supplement figure 1B.

claim: lncRNA1 initiates within HHV-6 origin of replication.
source: One lncRNA, designated here as lncRNA1, initiates within HHV-6 origin of replication (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: lncRNA1 resembles in synteny to an HCMV encoded lncRNA, RNA4.9.
source: One lncRNA, designated here as lncRNA1, initiates within HHV-6 origin of replication (Figure 4A) and therefore resembles in synteny to an HCMV encoded lncRNA, RNA4.9 although it is much shorter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of genomic locations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: lncRNA1 is the most highly expressed polyadenylated RNA in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B.
source: This transcript is the most highly expressed polyadenylated RNA in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The short ORF encoded by lncRNA1 contains the highest ribosome densities in the viral genomes.
source: This transcript is the most highly expressed polyadenylated RNA in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and its encoded short ORF, which contains the highest ribosome densities in the viral genomes (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on Ribo-seq data.

claim: lncRNA2 is a spliced transcript that partially overlaps U18.
source: The second lncRNA we identified, named here lncRNA2, is a spliced transcript that partially overlaps U18 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: lncRNA3 is transcribed between U77 and U79.
source: The third lncRNA, designated lncRNA3, is transcribed between U77 and U79 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: lncRNA3 has multiple possible isoforms generated by two alternative TSSs, two alternative polyadenylation sites, and alternative splicing.
source: This lncRNA has multiple possible isoforms generated by two alternative TSSs, two alternative polyadenylation sites, and alternative splicing.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: lncRNA3 is homologous to the HCMV encoded lncRNA5.0 and the Murine CMV encoded lncRNA7.2.
source: However by synteny, this lncRNA is homologous to the HCMV encoded lncRNA5.0 and the Murine CMV encoded lncRNA7.2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), shown to generate stable intronic RNAs which are not polyadenylated (Kulesza and Shenk, 2006; Kulesza and Shenk, 2004).
evidence: This is based on comparison of genomic locations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and supported by citations.

claim: HCMV lncRNA5.0 and Murine CMV lncRNA7.2 generate stable intronic RNAs which are not polyadenylated.
source: However by synteny, this lncRNA is homologous to the HCMV encoded lncRNA5.0 and the Murine CMV encoded lncRNA7.2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), shown to generate stable intronic RNAs which are not polyadenylated (Kulesza and Shenk, 2006; Kulesza and Shenk, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The intronic reads of lncRNA3 comprise less than 10% of what is expected from retained intron isoforms in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B.
source: To explore this possibility, we quantified the number of reads that span the exon-intron junction relative to the number of intronic reads, and found that in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B they comprise less than 10% of what is expected from retained intron isoforms (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The intronic reads of lncRNA3 do not seem to originate from intron retention and rather indicate that lncRNA3 generates a stable non-polyadenylated intron.
source: Therefore, these intronic reads do not seem to originate from intron retention and rather indicate that lncRNA3 also generates a stable non-polyadenylated intron.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data analysis and RT-qPCR results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The lncRNA3 intron was detected at significantly higher levels in cDNA synthesized using random hexamers compared to cDNA synthesized with poly(dT) oligomers.
source: Similar to the non-polyadenylated 18S ribosomal RNA, the intron RNA was detected at significantly higher levels in cDNA that was synthesized using random hexamers, while the polyadenylated lncRNA2 was more abundant or unchanged when poly(dT) oligomers were used in HHV-6A and HHV-6B, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The level of the intronic RNA of HHV-6B lncRNA3 is 100-fold higher than the spliced lncRNA3 based on RNA-seq analysis of total RNA.
source: We further quantified the abundance of the intronic RNA in of HHV-6B by deep sequencing total RNA without poly-A selection from infected cells. Based on these measurements the level of the intronic RNA of HHV-6B lncRNA3 is 100-fold higher than the spliced lncRNA3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), making it the most abundant transcript in infected cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data of total RNA shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The RNA5.0 intron is 10-fold higher than the spliced RNA5.0 in HCMV infected cells based on RNA-seq analysis of total RNA.
source: Similarly, RNA-seq analysis of total RNA from HCMV infected cells showed that the RNA5.0 intron is 10-fold higher than the spliced RNA5.0 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data of total RNA shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Northern blot analysis confirmed the presence of the HHV-6B lncRNA3 intron at the predicted size of ~1500 nt.
source: Additionally, we validated the presence of the HHV-6B lncRNA3 intron by performing Northern blot analysis, confirming the presence of the RNA at the predicted size of ~1500 nt (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on Northern blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The study trained a support vector machine (SVM) model to identify translation initiation sites based on Ribo-seq data sets.
source: To systematically define the full coding potential of HHV-6A and HHV-6B, we trained a support vector machine (SVM) model to identify translation initiation sites based on our Ribo-seq data sets, combining the actively translating ribosomes profile (CHX treatment), and initiation site enrichment (LTM and Harr) from cells infected with HHV-6 for 72 hr.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: The study found strong enrichment of translation initiation at the canonical AUG start codon.
source: In these sites, we found strong enrichment of translation initiation at the canonical AUG start codon, as well as weaker but still significant enrichment for the near-cognate start codons (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of predicted translation initiation sites shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CUG was the most common near-cognate start codon, similar to what was found in other herpesviruses and in human cells.
source: Of the near-cognate start codons, CUG was the most common, similar to what was found in other herpesviruses (Arias et al., 2014; Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012; Whisnant et al., 2019) and in human cells (Fields et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on analysis of predicted translation initiation sites and supported by citations.

claim: The study identified translation in 69 out of 88 HHV-6A ORFs and 63 out of 103 HHV-6B ORFs of previously annotated ORFs.
source: Of the previously annotated ORFs, we identified translation in 69 out of 88 HHV-6A ORFs and 63 out of 103 HHV-6B ORFs.
evidence: This is based on the SVM model predictions.

claim: The study identified 268 novel ORFs in HHV-6A and 216 novel ORFs in HHV-6B.
source: In total, we identified 268 novel ORFs in HHV-6A and 216 novel ORFs in HHV-6B (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on the SVM model predictions shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Newly identified ORFs are shorter than the annotated ones.
source: As expected, newly identified ORFs are shorter than the annotated ones (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C comparing size distributions.

claim: Many of the novel ORFs identified were very short (<20 aa, 141 in HHV-6A and 111 in HHV-6B).
source: Many of the novel ORFs we identified, were very short (<20 aa, 141 in HHV-6A and 111 in HHV-6B) and therefore are likely not functional at the polypeptide level.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the predicted ORFs.

claim: A large portion of the novel ORFs are iORFs, translated within other ORFs (80 ORFs in HHV-6A and 67 in HHV-6B).
source: In addition, a large portion of the remaining ORFs are iORFs, translated within other ORFs (80 ORFs in HHV-6A and 67 in HHV-6B, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the predicted ORFs shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The newly identified ORFs displayed three-nucleotide periodicity similar to previously annotated ORFs.
source: The newly identified ORFs displayed similar periodicity to the previously annotated ORFs, which was not seen in RNA-seq reads, further validating that these ORFs likely represent bona-fide translation products (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and is consistent with active translation.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of viral coding regions by footprint densities along infection revealed several distinct temporal expression patterns.
source: Hierarchical clustering of viral coding regions by footprint densities along infection (a measure of the relative translation rates) revealed several distinct temporal expression patterns (Figure 7A and see Figure 7—source data 1 for read numbers).
evidence: This is based on time-course Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cluster one contains ORFs whose expression is relatively high at 5hpi compared to 24 and 72hpi, and includes most of the genes classified as immediate-early (IE, U79, U90 and U95).
source: Cluster one contains ORFs whose expression is relatively high at 5hpi compared to 24 and 72hpi, and this cluster includes most of the genes classified as immediate-early (IE, U79, U90 and U95).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: U85, a glycoprotein previously classified as IE, was not efficiently translated at 5hpi and was assigned to cluster 2.
source: Another gene, U85, a glycoprotein previously classified as IE (Tsao et al., 2009), was not efficiently translated at 5hpi and was assigned to cluster 2.
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of time-course data and comparison with previous classification.

claim: Cluster two contains genes that are most highly expressed at 24hpi and is enriched in early genes.
source: Cluster two contains genes that are most highly expressed at 24hpi and is enriched in early genes.
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Clusters 3 and 4 contain genes that are mostly expressed at 72hpi and are both enriched in late genes.
source: Clusters 3 and 4 contain genes that are mostly expressed at 72hpi and are both enriched in late genes; however, cluster four is composed of genes that are expressed almost exclusively at 72hpi.
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The DNA helicase/primase U43 and the large tegument protein U31 were previously annotated as late genes, but reach peak translation at the 24hpi timepoint.
source: While most of the previously annotated late genes were assigned to these clusters, the DNA helicase/primase U43 and the large tegument protein U31 were previously annotated as late genes, but are shown here to reach peak translation at the 24hpi timepoint.
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of time-course data and comparison with previous annotations.

claim: Pervasive use of alternative 5' ends in HCMV transcripts is critical for the tight temporal regulation of viral gene expression and production of alternate protein products.
source: We previously demonstrated that pervasive use of alternative 5' ends in HCMV transcripts is critical for the tight temporal regulation of viral gene expression and production of alternate protein products (Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Similar temporal regulation of 5' ends was observed in HHV-6B genes including U53, U81/U82, and U51.
source: We observed similar phenomena in the temporal regulation of several HHV-6B genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 7B, 7C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The U53 gene contains newly identified iORFs that are translated more efficiently at 72hpi than at 24hpi relative to the main U53 ORF.
source: For example, the U53 gene contains newly identified iORFs, one of which initiates at an AUG, and is an orthologue of the annotated HHV-6A U53.5 ORF (Figure 7B). Relative to the main U53 ORF, these iORFs are translated more efficiently at 72hpi than at 24hpi.
evidence: This is based on time-course Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The same pattern of temporal regulation of iORFs was found in the HCMV homolog, UL80.
source: Notably, we found the same pattern in the HCMV homolog, UL80 (Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on comparison with HCMV data shown in Figure 7B and supported by a citation.

claim: uORFs are enriched in the 5'UTRs of late genes compared to earlier kinetic classes in both HHV-6A and HHV-6B.
source: For both HHV-6A and HHV-6B we found an enrichment of uORFs in the 5'UTRs of late genes compared to earlier kinetic classes (Figure 7D, p-value < 0.01, proportion test).
evidence: This is based on analysis of uORF distribution shown in Figure 7D with statistical testing.

claim: There was no enrichment for the presence of iORFs in any kinetic class.
source: In contrast, there was no enrichment for the presence of iORFs in any kinetic class (Figure 7E, p-value > 0.3)
evidence: This is based on analysis of iORF distribution shown in Figure 7E with statistical testing.

claim: uORFs but not iORFs are enriched in 5'UTRs of HCMV genes that are expressed with late kinetics.
source: We further extended this analysis to HCMV ORFs and found that uORFs but not iORFs are enriched in 5'UTRs of HCMV genes that are expressed with late kinetics, similar to what we see in HHV-6 (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of HCMV data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: An increased proportional use of non-canonical start codons occurs late in infection.
source: Interestingly, we also observed an increased proportional use of non-canonical start codons late in infection (Figure 7—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is based on analysis of start codon usage shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The number of iORFs and uORFs in HHV-6A and HHV-6B homolog ORFs are well correlated.
source: We found that the number of iORFs and uORFs in HHV-6A and HHV-6B homolog ORFs are well correlated, indicating a high level of conservation of these translation events between these two viruses (p<10−15 for uORFs and p<10−10 for iORFs, Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 8A with statistical testing.

claim: In five iORF-containing HHV-6 genes and in four uORF-containing HHV-6 genes, the HCMV homologs also contained similar iORFs or uORFs.
source: We also found some features that are conserved in HCMV. In five iORF-containing HHV-6 genes and in four uORF-containing HHV-6 genes, the HCMV homologs also contained similar iORFs or uORFs (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison with HCMV data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: U51 and its HCMV homolog UL78 contain a conserved uORF and show conserved kinetics along infection.
source: One of the HHV-6/HCMV homolog ORF pairs containing a conserved uORF is U51 and its HCMV homolog UL78 (Figure 8C), which interestingly also show conserved kinetics along infection suggesting a potential regulatory mechanism conserved between these viruses (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conserved presence of several uORFs and iORFs suggests that their occurrence is not random and likely represents a functional module that plays a role in regulating herpesvirus protein expression.
source: Altogether, the conserved presence of several uORFs and iORFs suggests that their occurrence is not random, and it is likely that these represent a functional module that plays a role in regulating herpesvirus protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation analysis.

claim: Traditional annotations of HHV-6 genomes are likely incomplete.
source: Taken together, this unforeseen complexity of herpesviruses suggests the current annotations of HHV-6 genomes are likely incomplete.
evidence: This is inferred from the discovery of hundreds of novel ORFs and other genomic features.

claim: The surplus of uORFs and their preferred use specifically at late time points of infection indicate that they may have a functional role in controlling viral gene expression, probably when cellular stress pathways are engaged.
source: The surplus of uORFs and their preferred use specifically at late time points of infection indicate that they may have a functional role in controlling viral gene expression, probably when cellular stress pathways are engaged.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of uORFs in late genes and knowledge about cellular stress responses.

claim: The high representation of sORFs, iORFs and uORFs in the viral genome, particularly at late stages of infection, is probably driven by extensive use of alternative transcription initiation and changes in translation permissiveness.
source: The overall high representation of sORFs, iORFs and uORFs in the viral genome, particularly at late stages of infection, is probably driven by several mechanisms; the first is extensive use of alternative transcription initiation, which is highly prevalent at late time point of infection with herpesviruses, and allows the translation of multiple translation products from the same viral loci (Balázs et al., 2018; Parida et al., 2019; Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012; Whisnant et al., 2019); the second mechanism may be related to changes in translation permissiveness which can explain the increase in translation initiation from near canonical start codons.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to related work.

claim: Unlike mammalian lncRNAs that are significantly less abundant than canonical mRNAs, in herpesviruses lncRNAs represent the most abundant group of viral transcripts.
source: Unlike mammalian lncRNAs, that as a group are significantly less abundant than canonical mRNAs (Mukherjee et al., 2017), in herpesviruses lncRNAs represent the most abundant group of viral transcripts (Gatherer et al., 2011; Tycowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: lncRNA1 resembles the HCMV RNA4.9 as both are transcribed from the viral origin of replication at the same orientation.
source: lncRNA1 resembles the HCMV RNA4.9 as both are transcribed from the viral origin of replication at the same orientation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of genomic locations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNA5.0 has previously been shown to generate a stable intron that is not required for HCMV replication in fibroblasts.
source: RNA5.0 has previously been shown to generate a stable intron that is not required for HCMV replication in fibroblasts (Kulesza and Shenk, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Mutant MCMV viruses lacking the stable intron RNA of the 7.2 kb ortholog of RNA5.0 replicated normally in culture, but exhibited a defect in establishing a persistent infection in vivo.
source: A murine cytomegalovirus 7.2 kb ortholog of RNA5.0 was identified which also generates a stable intronic RNA. Mutant MCMV viruses lacking this stable intron RNA replicated normally in culture, but exhibited a defect in establishing a persistent infection in vivo (Kulesza and Shenk, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The production of a stable intronic RNA from the lncRNA3 locus is a conserved feature of betaherpesviruses.
source: Our results indicate that the production of a stable intronic RNA from this locus is a conserved feature of betaherpesviruses, implying a central function.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation observed in HHV-6A, HHV-6B, HCMV, and MCMV.

claim: The intronic RNA of lncRNA3 is probably the main functional element in this locus.
source: The strong expression of the intronic RNA, which is 100-fold higher compared to the spliced RNA, and its conservation in beta herpesviruses points that this intronic RNA is probably the main functional element in this locus.
evidence: This is inferred from the high expression level and conservation.

claim: A small non-coding RNA (sncRNA-U77) that is mapped to the intron of lncRNA3 was shown to be expressed by HHV-6A.
source: Interestingly, a small non-coding RNA (sncRNA-U77) that is mapped to the intron of lncRNA3 was shown to be expressed by HHV-6A (Nukui et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: It is possible that the stable intron of lncRNA3 is further processed to create additional functional elements.
source: It is therefore possible that the stable intron is further processed to create additional functional elements.
evidence: This is speculated based on the existence of sncRNA-U77.

claim: TSA-mediated HHV-6A transactivation results in increased transcription from a region overlapping the lncRNA3 locus.
source: Furthermore, a recent study showed that TSA-mediated HHV-6A transactivation results in increased transcription from a region overlapping the lncRNA3 locus (Prusty et al., 2018a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: lncRNA3 may be involved in HHV-6A reactivation.
source: Furthermore, a recent study showed that TSA-mediated HHV-6A transactivation results in increased transcription from a region overlapping the lncRNA3 locus (Prusty et al., 2018a), implying lncRNA3 may be involved in HHV-6A reactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased transcription during reactivation.
